context: solar field + thermal storage + steam power block; mass assembly in the field, salt melting at start-up

brief.intro: New to this project type? A concentrated solar power plant uses mirrors to make heat, stores the heat, and then makes electricity with an ordinary steam turbine — so it can generate after sunset. In a tower plant, thousands of sun-tracking mirrors (heliostats) aim sunlight at a receiver on top of a tall tower; in a trough plant, long rows of curved mirrors heat oil in a pipe along their focus. The heat goes into molten salt held in two huge insulated tanks, hot and cold, and a steam generator uses it to drive the turbine. It is two projects in one: a solar field built by mass production — the same assembly repeated tens of thousands of times over square kilometres — and a compact, demanding thermal plant. The step newcomers don't expect is melting thousands of tonnes of salt and keeping every salt pipe hot so it never freezes.

must_get_right: Plan the solar field as a factory: assembly-line output per day, installation crews and alignment, tracked in units — it is the largest quantity and the easiest to underestimate.
The receiver tower (slip-formed concrete), the receiver itself and the salt tanks are the long single items; the tank foundations with their cooling pipes are specialised work.
Salt melting is a campaign of weeks needing a temporary melting plant, gas and the cold tank ready; heat tracing must be complete and tested first, or the salt freezes in the pipes.
The power block is a conventional steam plant with its own long-lead turbine and its own commissioning chain (steam blowing, synchronisation) that must meet the solar side at the right time.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The solar field is organised by zone and planned by production rate; the tower, storage and power block are organised by area and system.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar; high-wind days stop mirror installation and tower lifts, and are allowed for. Salt melting runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Grading → foundations → collector assembly and installation by zone → alignment. In parallel: tower → receiver; tanks → salt piping → heat tracing → insulation; power block → steam piping. Then salt melting → salt circulation → receiver start-up → steam blowing → synchronisation → storage tests → performance test. The critical path runs through the turbine, the tower and receiver, or the salt system.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The grid connection is ready for back-energisation; gas or fuel is available for salt melting and the auxiliary boiler; mirror supply sustains the assembly rate.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Molten salt (thousands of tonnes) & salt pumps

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Very large site with long travel distances; wind limits; mirror breakage and dust; work at height on the tower; hot-salt safety rules after melting.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: solar-field productivity, wind delays, heat-tracing defects causing salt freezing, tank foundation or tank leaks, late turbine or receiver, and performance below guarantee. Contingency is held before salt melting and before the performance test.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by solar-field zone, area and system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the assembly, installation and piping crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
